newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland's McCreevy warns of risks to inflation.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's McCreevy warns of risks to inflation.

text.p: Irish finance minister Charlie McCreevy said on Tuesday that there were risks on the inflation front and excessive wage expectations could add to those pressures.

"I am thinking here of the recent decline in the Effective Exchange Rate of the Irish pound, the huge increase in property prices and suggestions that tender prices for construction contracts in both the public and private sectors are growing rapidly," he said.

There were other signs of inflationary pressure such as the difficulties arising in some parts of the labour market in filling jobs, McCreevy told the second quarterly meeting to monitor implementation of the national wage agreement, Partnership 2000.
He said that all sides involved in determining the future development of the Irish economy had to be realistic and keep expectations in check.

"Ireland is running well at present in a fiercely competitive international race and is facing the next series of hurdles in fine shape. Don't put too much weight on her back and don't expect her to go too fast," he said, using a racing analogy.

McCreevy said the government would honour the tax commitments made in Partnership 2000. The previous government pledged tax reductions of one billion punts over a three-year period when negotiating the accord.
But McCreevy said that he would have to bear in mind the need to avoid adding to inflationary pressures in settling on the scale of the tax package in the next two budgets.
He also said that in his next two budgets he would set out fiscal targets to the year 2000 which would involve the elimination of Exchequer borrowing over the next two to three years.

"This more ambitious target will be facilitated by the lower deficit this year and the continuing high tax revenue buoyancy. As a country, we simply have to stop borrowing at a time when the economy is booming," McCreevy said.
He said the general government deficit this year would be below one percent of GDP, thanks to the continuing strong performance of the economy.
